title: A Mighty Wind
full_review:
"A Mighty Wind" (Warner Bros.) is a modest, mock-documentary-style comedy about three washed-up folk groups whose aging members are reunited after decades for a hootenanny to commemorate the man who shepherded them to near-stardom.

As in his past films, "This Is Spinal Tap" (1984), "Waiting for Guffman" (1996) and "Best in Show" (2000), director Christopher Guest plays impresario to a hilariously talented ensemble, including such usual suspects as Bob Balaban, Eugene Levy, Michael McKean and Catherine O'Hara. Guest and company's wry and mostly improvisational repartee once again good-naturedly pokes fun at a stratum of American culture without stooping to vulgarities, and in doing so proves that funny bones need not be offended to be tickled.

When folk icon Irving Steinbloom passes away, his son Jonathan (Balaban) decides to organize a one-night-only memorial concert in New York City's Town Hall to celebrate his dad's legacy. Headlining the event are the legendary promoter's three favorite groups -- though many of the musicians have not performed together for years.

Billed to appear are the New Main Street Singers (featuring John Michael Higgins, Jane Lynch and Parker Posey), the colorful kings of the amusement park circuit, as well as the Folksmen (Guest, McKean and Harry Shearer), whose meteoric rise to the "middle of the charts" was derailed by a label which cut corners by not punching holes in the center of their LPs. The highlight of the evening is the much-anticipated reunion of Mitch & Mickey (Levy and O'Hara), once the poster couple for young love, whose soured relationship drove Mickey into the arms of a catheter salesman and Mitch to the funny farm.

Jonathan, anal-retentive but well-intentioned, has hired a stunningly inept PR firm for publicizing the gala, the Zipken Group (Jennifer Coolidge and Larry Miller), who know next to nothing about folk music and even less about public relations. But the times, they are a-changing -- and, after 30 years, this oddball assembly has one night to share a stage, mend personal antagonisms, and bask in the spotlight of bygone mediocrity.

The performances are so genuinely funny that it doesn't matter that some of the material seems retread from earlier films. While not as forthcoming in its humor as the 1984 cult classic "This is Spinal Tap," fans will be relieved to find that Guest's musical taste has remained abysmally (read hilariously) bad, offering such outrageous parodies as "Blood on the Coal," "Potato's in the Paddy Wagon" and the stirring ballad "Never Did No Wanderin" about a man who didn't do anything (all of which should spawn a folk-spoofing companion album). Though much of the film plays like Spinal Tap unplugged, "A Mighty Wind" still pays high-chuckle dividends with such droll zingers as "Doing 'then' now would be retro, but doing 'then' then was very nowtro."

The cast members seem to sincerely like the characters they play -- evident in the screwball yet ultimately endearing portrayal of the motley misfits. Unlike Guest's previous works, this film is not without a genuinely tender moment -- at the climax of Mitch & Mickey's signature hit, "A Kiss at the End of the Rainbow," they exchange a heartfelt kiss after 28 years of estrangement.

The troupe is uniformly superb, but special mention belongs to Fred Willard for his zany Mike LaFontaine, the off-the-wall manager of the New Main Street Singers, and Levy for his restrained and benignly-psychotic, dead-pan Mitch.

You might not want to let this "Mighty Wind" blow you by.

Due to some sex-related humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned that some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
